EXCLUSIVE: Baseball legend Mariano Rivera on Yankees '90s Dynasty, Core 4, pressure of playing in NYC and his new Mo's Hot Sauce appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
When the ninth inning arrived in the Bronx, nothing was more intimidating for opposing hitters than Mariano Rivera jogging out of the bullpen with his iconic "Enter Sandman" entrance music playing. Over 19 seasons with the New York Yankees, Rivera established himself as the greatest closer of all time, retiring as MLB's career leader with 652 saves. The first player ever unanimously elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame, Rivera was at his best when the stakes were highest, helping anchor a Yankees dynasty that won five World Series championships during his career.
From his virtually unhittable cutter to his unmatched composure in October, Rivera became synonymous with dominance in the ninth inning. He recorded an MLB-record 42 postseason saves and a remarkable 0.70 ERA across 141 playoff innings, playing an integral role alongside Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, and Jorge Posada in a homegrown group that became known as the Yankees' "Core Four."
Baseball legend Mariano Rivera with ClutchPoints' Rob Lepelstat for an exclusive interview in the Bronx, NY – just minutes from Yankee Stadium, where Mo spent his entire 19-year MLB career with the Yankees
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
More than a decade after throwing his final pitch, Rivera's impact continues to extend beyond the mound. The Yankees legend has entered the hot sauce business with Mo's Heat, his new hot sauce brand that gives Rivera an opportunity to bring his competitive mentality into a completely different arena while connecting with fans in a new way.
During an exclusive interview with ClutchPoints' Rob Lepelstat, Rivera discussed the inspiration behind Mo's Hot Sauce, revealed the mentality that allowed him to thrive in baseball's biggest moments, reflected on the Yankees' iconic 1990s dynasty and his relationship with the Core Four, opened up about playing alongside "The Captain" Derek Jeter, and shared his advice for today's Yankees as they attempt to bring a 28th World Series championship to the Bronx.
Mo's Hot Sauce
Baseball legend Mariano Rivera made a career out of bringing the heat in the ninth inning. Now, the legendary New York Yankees closer is doing it in a much different way.
Rivera has entered the hot sauce business with Mo's Hot Sauce, adding another venture to a résumé that already includes five World Series championships, a unanimous Baseball Hall of Fame induction, MLB's all-time saves record (652) and recognition as the greatest closer in the history of the sport.
Mariano is proud of his roots, which is why Mo's Heat features authentic Panamanian flavors, hand-selected habanero peppers, and all-natural ingredients from their 122-year-old hot sauce recipe.
It includes three flavors: The Sinker, The Curve and the signature sauce, The Cutter (of course!), named after Rivera's unhittable pitch.
The venture is about more than simply putting his famous name on a bottle. He explained the motivation behind Mo's Hot Sauce and why he believes the product can stand out in a crowded market.
"This product is something special for me, dear to my heart, so I'm happy that we could come up with this," Rivera described. "It's all what you put in there, you know? Besides the ingredients, you have to put love and passion in there, you know, commitment. And—and that's what we have done. You know, besides all the ingredients that are in there, all-natural, by the way, I mean, we're putting a lot of effort, a lot of passion, love, and commitment to make sure that the fans and people love this sauce. Not because Mariano, but because of the sauce."
From the Mo's Heat website: Made with highly selected habanero peppers and spices using a 122-year-old recipe, Mo's Heat hot sauces offer a unique flavor and aroma to enhance any meal. As an MLB pitcher, Mariano Rivera played every game for his home country, Panama. And he founded Mo's Heat to celebrate their flavor, character, and fire.
Fans can find out more information, including where to buy, pricing, and flavors, at https://mosheatsauces.com/.
The Closer Mentality
When the Yankees needed three outs to close out a game, there was nobody they trusted more than Rivera.
The numbers speak for themselves. Rivera finished his career as MLB's all-time saves leader with 652, but his dominance became even more pronounced when the lights were brightest. In 96 postseason appearances, Rivera recorded 42 saves while allowing just 11 earned runs, good for the lowest ERA in playoff history (0.70).
Yet Rivera's greatness wasn't simply the product of his famous cutter. His ability to remain calm in moments that could overwhelm even the best players became as much a part of his reputation as the pitch itself.
Rivera explained how he approached those pressure-packed situations and what allowed him to maintain the same mentality whether he was pitching in a regular-season game or trying to record the final outs of a World Series.
"I tried to simplify the game, I tried to simplify the way I pitch… If I can get you out in one pitch, I would try to do that. I wasn't afraid of contact."
That mindset helped Rivera become synonymous with the closer position and gave the Yankees an enormous advantage during their championship years: When No. 42 entered the game, everyone in the ballpark knew exactly what was coming — and hitters still struggled to stop it.
Rivera's Cutter
Few weapons in sports history carry the mythic status of Mariano Rivera's cut fastball. Thrown with effortless arm speed and late, violent movement, the pitch shattered hundreds of bats—and just as many opposing rallies—en route to a record 652 career saves, and five World Series rings.
Hitters across Major League Baseball spent nearly two decades studying tape, anticipating the pitch, and bracing for it, yet virtually none could solve it. Ironically, the most unhittable pitch in baseball history wasn't engineered in a lab or perfected through endless trial and error; it was a divine accident that Rivera discovered while trying to do the exact opposite.
Rivcera's cutter came out of the exact same arm slot and had the same visual spin as his standard fastball. Batters had only roughly 0.17 seconds to react and could not tell the difference until it was too late.
The ball traveled at up to 90–95 mph and would break sharply by up to 8 inches, usually in the final 10 feet before reaching the plate.
Rivera threw the cutter roughly 88% of the time later in his career, per MLB.com. Hitters knew it was coming for nearly two decades, yet they still could not hit it.
When asked about the origin of his signature weapon, the Hall of Fame closer reflected on how a frustrating bullpen session with pitching coach Mel Stottlemyre ultimately gave birth to baseball perfection.
"It was God-given for sure, because we were trying to stop it from moving… I told [Mel Stottlemyre], 'Hey man, whatever's gonna happen is gonna happen, because I have no control of this pitch, let's leave it.'
The rest is history.
The Yankees' 1990s Dynasty
The Yankees' championship run of the late 1990s remains one of the greatest stretches by any team in modern baseball history.
After winning the World Series in 1996, New York put together a historic 1998 season before completing a three-peat with championships in 1999 and 2000. Over a five-season span, the Yankees won four World Series titles and established a dynasty that has yet to be replicated in MLB since.
Rivera was there for all of it.
Before becoming the Yankees' closer, Rivera played a crucial setup role during the 1996 championship season. Once he took over the ninth inning, he became one of the foundational pieces of a team that seemingly expected to be playing deep into October every year.
Looking back on those teams, Rivera reflected on what made that group so successful and why the Yankees were able to consistently perform when the stakes were at their highest.
The championships featured countless memorable moments, but Rivera believes the culture surrounding those Yankees teams was just as important as the talent on the roster.
"There was a—a commitment and—and a passion and love with 25 players. Well, before was the—the owner, you know, Mr. George was amazing, and then uh the coaching staff that they put together, Joe and—and the rest of the play—the rest of the coaches. And then the players. You know, I mean, we were family, we were a team, we were family. And that makes a lot of difference. You know, we don't—we don't try to separate ourselves, we try to unify ourselves even tighter, tighter and tighter. And as results, we have four championships in five years."
The Core 4
As the Yankees continued winning, four homegrown players became constants in the Bronx: Rivera, Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, and Jorge Posada.
Eventually dubbed the "Core Four," the group came through the Yankees organization together before becoming central figures in one of the most successful eras in franchise history. Rivera, Jeter, Pettitte, and Posada were teammates for five World Series championships, with their careers becoming permanently intertwined in Yankees history.
What made the group unique wasn't simply its success. Each player filled a distinctly different role, yet all four shared the experience of growing from prospects into established stars while dealing with the expectations that came with playing in New York.
Rivera reflected on his relationship with Jeter, Pettitte, and Posada and what it meant to experience so much of his career alongside the same group of teammates.
"We're talking about family. We're not talking about teammates or players… We grew up together, coming from the minor league system all the way to the big leagues… We were just brainwashed: 'We need to win regardless.' It's not about second place, it's about winning the whole thing."
Years after their final game together, the Core Four remains synonymous with an era when October baseball in the Bronx felt almost inevitable.
The Captain, Derek Jeter
Within that Core Four, Rivera shared an especially remarkable journey with Derek Jeter.
Both made their MLB debuts in 1995. Neither could have known at the time that they would spend nearly two decades together and eventually become two of the most recognizable Yankees of their generation.
Jeter became the captain and face of the franchise. Rivera became the greatest closer in baseball history. Together, they were fixtures on five championship teams and experienced virtually everything the sport had to offer.
Their partnership also produced one of the most memorable moments of Rivera's final season. During his last appearance at Yankee Stadium in 2013, Jeter and Pettitte walked to the mound to remove an emotional Rivera from the game.
Rivera discussed what made Jeter such a special teammate and leader and what stood out about playing alongside him for so many years.
"Derek was the perfect captain because he had us… three players, teammates, that loved him and were willing to do whatever it takes to make him look good. He was the face, he had to be in the media talking about it, but we were all doing the job."
For all their individual accomplishments, their careers will forever be linked by what they accomplished together in pinstripes.
Rivera's Advice for Today's Yankees
More than a decade after Rivera threw his final pitch, the standard in the Bronx remains the same.
Winning games isn't enough. Making the postseason isn't enough. For the Yankees, success is ultimately measured in championships.
Rivera understands that pressure better than almost anyone. He experienced the expectations that came with wearing the pinstripes while playing for teams that didn't just reach October — they expected to win once they got there.
Today's Yankees face the challenge of creating their own championship legacy while playing under the weight of that history. Rivera offered his advice for the current roster and explained what it takes to succeed in New York when expectations are at their highest.
"They know the advice. It's just—just you have to push. You have to keep pushing and pushing and pushing to get it done, because I mean, this thing is not easy. People know that winning championships is not easy at all. So, we have the team, we have the players, so we just have to have the determination and the passion to get it done, you know? However, you have to get it done, you have to find a way to get it done, and that's what we're doing."
The names and faces have changed since Rivera's championship years, but the goal hasn't. For a franchise with 27 World Series titles, the winningest team in North American professional sports history, the expectation will always be to add another one.
—
Related: This bold Aaron Judge take may cause Yankees fans to raise eyebrows

item.content:encoded:
TAMPA, Florida — Se suponía que la mansión frente al mar que Derek Jeter construyó en Davis Islands iba a desaparecer. Sin embargo, años después de que se concediera el permiso de demolición y se presentaran los planos para una casa nueva mucho más grande, la antigua finca del ex capitán de los Yankees sigue en pie.
Un nuevo informe publicado este jueves ha vuelto a sacar a la luz la insólita historia que rodea a la propiedad situada en el número 58 de Bahama Circle, una enorme mansión de Tampa que en su día fue de Jeter y que más tarde alquilaron Tom Brady y Gisele Bündchen. La atención se centra ahora en una pregunta que lleva rondando desde que salió a la luz un plan de demolición en 2022: ¿por qué sigue ahí la mansión?
La respuesta sigue sin estar clara. Pero la información pública sobre la propiedad y los permisos muestra que la historia es más complicada que el simple caso de una casa abandonada destinada a la demolición.
Jeter construye una de las casas más famosas de Tampa
Según Mansion Global, Jeter reunió tres parcelas contiguas frente al mar en 2005 y 2006 por unos 7,7 millones de dólares. Después encargó la construcción a medida de la finca, creando así una de las casas más grandes y reconocibles del sur de Tampa.
La propiedad ocupa unas 1,2 acres y cuenta con 345 pies de frente de mar en la bahía de Hillsborough. Según Realtor.com, la vivienda tiene una superficie de 21.796 pies cuadrados, con siete dormitorios y 16 baños. La finca también incluye una piscina de agua salada de 80 pies, amplios porches y balcones, un embarcadero con elevadores para barcos, una sala de cine, un gimnasio y otras comodidades de lujo.
Su fama creció aún más en 2020, cuando Brady y Bundchen alquilaron la casa después de que Brady dejara los New England Patriots para fichar por los Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Al final, Jeter puso la propiedad a la venta por 29 millones de dólares. La venta se cerró en mayo de 2021 por 22,5 millones de dólares, lo que supuso, según Mansion Global, la transacción residencial más cara de la zona de Tampa Bay en aquel momento. El comprador utilizó un fideicomiso y, en aquel momento, no se reveló públicamente quién era el propietario beneficiario.
El plan de demolición deja a la mansión en una situación precaria
El siguiente capítulo de la mansión parecía estar escrito en septiembre de 2022, cuando se concedió una licencia de demolición residencial para la propiedad. La perspectiva de derribar una casa que se había vendido por más de 22 millones de dólares llamó la atención de todo el país por su tamaño, su historia ligada a famosos y su ubicación frente al mar.
Luego surgió un plan aún más ambicioso. En octubre de 2023, el Tampa Bay Times informó de que Ellison Construction se estaba preparando para sustituir la mansión construida por Jeter por una residencia de unos 30 000 pies cuadrados. Se esperaba que la casa propuesta contara con seis dormitorios, nueve baños completos, 11 aseos, un gimnasio, una piscina y más zonas verdes.
En ese momento, se preveía que la construcción comenzara en 2024 y durara unos tres años.
Pero la mansión original nunca se derribó. En junio de 2026, el Tampa Bay Times informó de que la casa seguía en pie, a pesar de que se había solicitado un permiso de demolición años antes. La propiedad volvió a llamar la atención esta semana cuando nuevas noticias destacaron la transformación, que parecía estar estancada.
Los registros de permisos complican el último misterio
Hay un detalle en las últimas versiones que hay que tener en cuenta. El historial de la remodelación no se quedó en silencio tras la licencia de demolición de 2022.
El historial de la propiedad de Realtor.com muestra una solicitud de nueva construcción residencial y ampliaciones con fecha del 22 de noviembre de 2023, con categorías de obra que incluyen una ampliación de la vivienda, la construcción de una piscina y un spa, y la construcción residencial. Ese mismo historial muestra una prórroga del permiso residencial concedida el 20 de noviembre de 2024.
Esas entradas no explican por qué la mansión actual sigue en pie, ni aclaran cuándo o si se terminará la construcción de la nueva vivienda anunciada. Sin embargo, sí muestran que se siguieron tramitando permisos tras la solicitud original de demolición.
Esa distinción es importante porque un informe publicado el jueves afirmaba que no se solicitaron nuevos permisos tras la caducidad del permiso de demolición. El historial de permisos, al que se puede acceder públicamente, indica lo contrario.
Por ahora, la conclusión más plausible es también la más sencilla: el calendario de demolición y remodelación anunciado para la propiedad no se ha desarrollado como se esperaba en un principio, y la mansión sigue en pie.
El rastro de la propiedad añade otra capa inusual
La titularidad de la propiedad también ha contribuido a mantener el misterio. En informaciones anteriores se identificó al titular de la escritura como Zebb.com Trust. El Tampa Bay Times señaló en 2023 que «Zebb.com» era el nombre de una aplicación de criptomonedas y mencionó su relación con ZebPay, una plataforma de intercambio de criptomonedas.
Esa relación ha llevado a algunos informes recientes a describir la propiedad como perteneciente a un fideicomiso de criptomonedas. Los registros públicos son más precisos en cuanto a la estructura jurídica de la propiedad que en cuanto a quién se beneficia en última instancia del fideicomiso.
En un aviso del impuesto sobre bienes inmuebles del condado de Hillsborough de 2025, David L. Koche figura como fideicomisario de 58 Bahama Circle. El hecho de que un fideicomisario aparezca en los registros inmobiliarios no establece, por sí solo, la identidad del propietario beneficiario del fideicomiso.
Por su parte, Jeter ya no es dueño de la mansión desde que la vendió en 2021 y no tiene ningún papel documentado públicamente en las decisiones actuales sobre la demolición o la remodelación.
El nombre de Jeter sigue ahí, ya que la mansión no se va a desaparecer
Cinco años después de que Jeter la vendiera, la propiedad de Davis Islands sigue estando vinculada a él por su tamaño y su historia deportiva. Él la construyó. Brady la alquiló. La casa batió un récord de ventas en Tampa Bay. Después, sus nuevos propietarios se propusieron derribarla y construir algo aún más grande.
La licencia de demolición, el proyecto de construcción de un nuevo edificio de 30.000 pies cuadrados y los trámites posteriores para obtener nuevas licencias apuntan todos hacia una remodelación. Sin embargo, lo que más llama la atención en 2026 se ve desde la calle y desde el agua: la antigua mansión de Jeter sigue ahí.
Hasta que los propietarios o los constructores expliquen los cambios en el calendario —o hasta que por fin empiece la demolición—, una de las casas más famosas que jamás se haya relacionado con una estrella de los Yankees seguirá siendo una historia inmobiliaria sin resolver.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' No. 1 prospect, shortstop George Lombard Jr., recently revealed that he had the chance to get some tips from Derek Jeter earlier this year.
Lombard, MLB Pipeline's No. 13 overall prospect for 2026, met up with Jeter in January, according to The Athletic's Brendan Kuty, months before the 21-year-old even made his Triple-A debut, let alone his first game in the Bronx. The young shortstop reportedly asked the Hall of Famer about playing for the Yankees and in the majors, among other topics. But one suggestion from the 14-time All-Star really stuck with the top prospect: "be a stand-up dude."
"Whether that's in the clubhouse or with the media or the fans, whatever it is. Be authentic and be a good person," Lombard said Jeter told him, according to Kuty. "It goes a long way, doing those little things. Whether that's always being upfront and honest or remembering people's names. Just being an overall good human being. It keeps you grounded and keeps you humble and it allows you to keep doing the stuff on the field and producing on the field and helping out the team wherever you can, while keeping all the unnecessary distractions away."
How has George Lombard Jr.'s first stint in the majors gone so far?
Many New York fans will probably be thrilled to hear that Lombard has already been trying to learn from a Yankees legend like Jeter. So far, though, it hasn't been all smooth sailing for the 21-year-old in the majors.
In his first 32 MLB games, Lombard is hitting .218 (24-for-110) with three home runs and 11 RBIs. The highly touted defender also went through an unexpected streak of six straight games with an error in August. While his defense has looked better lately, the 6-foot-2 shortstop has faced some adversity in his first stint in the big leagues.
The Yankees recently recalled Anthony Volpe to play second base for the first time in the majors after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list. So, New York appears to be sticking with Lombard at shortstop for now. And with the Yankees clinching a playoff spot on Monday, the top prospect should get his first taste of October baseball in the Bronx soon.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — George Lombard Jr. se encontraba en medio de la última celebración de los Yankees el lunes por la noche, con la cerveza chorreándole por la gorra y tras haber dado uno de los golpes más importantes de su joven carrera.
El novato campocorto abrió la octava entrada en el Target Field con un doble ante Andrew Morris, mandando una bola rápida de 98 mph hacia el centro-izquierdo cuando los Yankees iban perdiendo 2-1 ante los Minnesota Twins. A eso le siguieron seis carreras. Aaron Judge conectó el jonrón de tres carreras que sentenció el partido, y Nueva York se llevó la victoria por 8-3, asegurándose así otro viaje a octubre.
Tim Hill se llevó la victoria, Morris cargó con la derrota y John Schreiber se anotó el salvamento. Los Yankees mejoraron su balance a 87-63 y se colocaron a 3,5 partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Los Yankees le han pedido a un novato de 21 años que aprenda a jugar en la posición del cuadro más exigente de la organización en plena lucha por el título. En su debut en las Grandes Ligas, conectó un jonrón y brilló en defensa. Unas semanas más tarde, cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos y sufrió un bajón ofensivo que puso a prueba su capacidad de adaptación.
El lunes volvió a mostrar su otra cara. Lombard se fue con 1 de 4, anotó la carrera del empate y ayudó a encender la remontada que llevó a los Yankees a la postemporada por novena vez en diez temporadas. Ese hit le dejó con un total de 24 de 110, un promedio de .218, con tres jonrones y 11 carreras impulsadas.
Quizá la pregunta más importante para los Yankees sea cómo aprenderá Lombard a lidiar con todo lo que conlleva este puesto antes de que octubre le ponga aún más en el punto de mira.
Esa presión ya es una realidad. Los Yankees ven a Lombard como parte del equipo actual, no solo como una promesa a la que le dan minutos de juego en septiembre, y cada error o cada avance tiene ahora consecuencias en partidos que cuentan.
Una conversación de enero que ahora se ve de otra manera
Meses antes de que Lombard supiera que iba a ser el shortstop titular de los Yankees, se sentó a desayunar en Miami con Derek Jeter.
La cita la organizó un amigo común, según Brendan Kuty, de The Athletic, que dio a conocer los detalles el martes. Lombard se estaba preparando para los entrenamientos de primavera y iba a empezar la temporada en la Doble A.
Kuty destacó el doble del lunes como otra muestra de por qué los Yankees siguen apostando por el potencial de Lombard.
«Fue una demostración de ese talento natural para batear que hace que los Yankees tengan tan buena opinión de Lombard», escribió Kuty.
Pero lo más revelador de la reunión no tuvo mucho que ver con batear. Lombard dijo que la conversación versó sobre la vida con los Yankees, los medios de comunicación, las exigencias fuera del campo y la responsabilidad que conlleva ser una figura tan conocida en Nueva York.
«En Nueva York, el rendimiento en el campo es súper importante», dijo Lombard. «Pero tu carácter y cómo eres como persona son igual de importantes».
Ese mensaje ha cobrado más relevancia de lo que ninguno de los dos jugadores podría haber imaginado en enero.
Una prueba de resistencia de 42 días da un nuevo peso a la lección de Jeter
Solo 42 días separaron el debut de Lombard, el 4 de agosto, del 15 de septiembre. En ese tiempo, 32 partidos de las Grandes Ligas ya han traído consigo ese tipo de altibajos que pueden marcar la diferencia en la temporada de un novato en Nueva York.
Lombard empezó el 2026 en la Doble A, fue subiendo hasta la Triple A y llegó a los Yankees el 4 de agosto. Con 21 años y 63 días, se convirtió en el jugador más joven de los Yankees en ser titular como campocorto desde Jeter, que tenía 20 años y 350 días cuando fue titular en esa posición el 11 de junio de 1995.
Los Yankees no te lo pusieron fácil a Lombard para entrar en la plantilla. Le dieron el puesto de campo corto justo en plena lucha por los playoffs.
Bateó un jonrón en su debut. El 9 de septiembre, conectó el primer grand slam de los Yankees de la temporada y se convirtió en el jugador más joven de los Yankees en batear uno desde Mickey Mantle. El lunes, tras otra racha complicada al bate, conectó el doble que dio inicio a la entrada decisiva en Minnesota.
Su rendimiento irregular sigue formando parte de la evaluación. Al comenzar el lunes, Lombard tenía un promedio de .215, un OPS de .619 y un wRC+ de 73. En defensa ha demostrado la potencia de brazo y el alcance que lo convirtieron en el mejor prospecto de la organización, pero su racha de seis partidos con errores puso de manifiesto lo implacable que puede ser esa posición.
Ahí es donde la comparación con Jeter cobra importancia. Los Yankees están viendo cómo responde Lombard cuando el éxito, el fracaso y la atención llegan casi al mismo tiempo.
Boone ve algo más allá de los consejos sobre béisbol
Aaron Boone vio la decisión de Lombard de acudir a Jeter como una muestra de la curiosidad del novato por la franquicia y por su puesto.
El entrenador le dijo a The Athletic que valora a los jugadores que quieren entender la historia y la importancia de la organización de los Yankees. Lombard no buscó a Jeter solo para que le diera consejos técnicos. Quería saber cómo se las apañaba Jeter en la propia ciudad de Nueva York.
«Me encanta cuando a nuestros jugadores les interesa sentirse parte de la organización», dijo el entrenador de los Yankees. «Hacer algo así e ir a hablar con Derek… son cosas geniales, cuando tus jugadores muestran curiosidad. Mira, no todo el mundo es así. Hay que respetarlo. Pero te encanta cuando los chicos sienten curiosidad, entienden la importancia de esta organización y quieren formar parte importante de ella».
Aun así, Lombard dijo que la reunión con Jeter le pareció diferente. Las preguntas más importantes giraron en torno a cómo lidiar con el revuelo que rodeaba al partido.
El segundo mensaje de Jeter llega con el final de octubre
La relación no se quedó solo en el desayuno.
Jeter volvió al Yankee Stadium el viernes para los actos que conmemoraban el 25.º aniversario del 11 de septiembre. Visitó el vestuario de los Yankees y volvió a encontrarse con Lombard, que ya no era un joven promesa que soñaba con el puesto, sino el novato que lo ocupaba.
Lombard dijo que Jeter se alegró por él y le dio otro mensaje conciso.
«Ha sido un año un poco de locos», dijo Lombard. «Pero él se alegra por mí y me ha dicho que siga a lo mío y que no pierda la concentración».
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero Lombard sigue aprendiendo mientras el equipo persigue a Tampa Bay por el título de la división. Su bate aún tiene que mejorar. En defensa, puede pasar de estar impecable a cometer errores costosos.
Jeter no puede hacer esos ajustes por él. Lo que le ofreció a Lombard fue un marco de referencia para desenvolverse en esa posición mientras los va haciendo.
Para los Yankees, eso puede ser tan importante como cualquier cambio en el swing que el novato haga antes de octubre.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — As Derek Jeter spoke, George Lombard Jr. listened.
It was January in Miami, and a mutual friend had set up a meeting between Jeter, the legendary New York Yankees shortstop, and Lombard, then the club’s top shortstop prospect. Over breakfast, Jeter answered Lombard’s questions about life in the big leagues and life with the Yankees, and offered advice.
Advertisement
On Monday, in an interview with The Athletic in the visitors clubhouse at Target Field, Lombard could still vividly recall the morning he spent with the Hall of Famer.
Jeter was “a great dude” and “a normal dude,” Lombard said. He was also “humble and down to earth.”
But as Lombard reminisced, one piece of advice from Jeter, in particular, stood out.
“The big one — and it seems pretty simple and probably one of the most important things — is to be a stand-up dude,” Lombard said Jeter told him.
“Whether that’s in the clubhouse or with the media or the fans, whatever it is. Be authentic and be a good person. It goes a long way, doing those little things. Whether that’s always being upfront and honest or remembering people’s names. Just being an overall good human being. It keeps you grounded and keeps you humble and it allows you to keep doing the stuff on the field and producing on the field and helping out the team wherever you can, while keeping all the unnecessary distractions away.”
Lombard played a major role in Monday’s 8-3 victory over the Minnesota Twins, which came after a loss by the Toronto Blue Jays that clinched a spot in the playoffs for the Yankees.
In the eighth inning, the Yankees were losing 2-1 when Lombard crushed Andrew Morris’ 98 mph fastball for a double off the wall in left-center field. He moved to third on an infield single and then scored on José Caballero’s one-out hit up the middle.
“It was unbelievable,” Aaron Judge said of Lombard’s clutch hit. “I saw him, even leading up to that at-bat, he was on the iPad. He’s doing his homework. First-pitch swinging to be able to do that off a guy like that who has been so lock-down for the Twins all year was impressive.”
This double was the hardest hit ball of George Lombard Jr.’s career ‼️
(Details below) pic.twitter.com/3sobpw6ONV
— Jacob P.M.🌔 (@JacobBSpeaks) September 15, 2026
It was a display of the kind of natural hitting ability that has the Yankees so high on Lombard, who they hope will take over as shortstop of the future the way Jeter did in 1996.
Advertisement
At the time of their January meeting, neither Jeter nor Lombard could have known how soon he would potentially be following in Jeter’s footsteps. Still, Lombard jumped at the chance to make a connection with Jeter, now 52.
Lombard, 21, wasn’t exactly new to meeting great players. As the son of retired outfielder and current Detroit Tigers bench coach George Lombard Sr., he used to take ground balls at Dodger Stadium next to Corey Seager, mimicking his movements. He also used to run around the outfield with a young Cody Bellinger, now one of his teammates.
But meeting Jeter was different, Lombard said.
“There definitely was some emotion involved in all that,” he recalled. “You’re going to go talk to Derek Jeter. I don’t know if I was nervous, but I was excited and looking forward to it.”
Lombard said Jeter was immediately cool with him “picking his brain and talking about his experiences.” They talked about “everything.”
“I think the better questions — and the ones that are more valuable — are all the non-baseball (questions),” Lombard said. “How he approached dealing with New York. Dealing with everything that comes with it. The media. The off-the-field stuff. How, in his case, being the captain, dealing with all of those responsibilities. All of it. Just good conversation. Very insightful. Definitely someone that you can take a lot from having a short conversation.”
To Lombard, Jeter stressed the importance of having a strong character.
“In New York, the on-field impact is extremely important,” Lombard said. “But the character and who you are person-wise is just as important.”
Derek Jeter & George Lombard Jr.’s swing comparisons are nearly IDENTICAL 👀🤯 pic.twitter.com/MRjyuGLHeW
— Concrete City Sports (@concretecityccs) August 11, 2026
Back then, Lombard was preparing for major-league spring training, and he would begin the season in Double A. But after dominating there and eventually acing his Triple-A assignment, he was called up by the Yankees on Aug. 4 — right after the trade deadline — and was asked to take over shortstop and also help their push to the playoffs. At the time, he was the youngest player in franchise history since Jeter to start at shortstop, at 21 years and 63 days old. Jeter was just 20 years and 350 days old when he debuted as a starting shortstop on June 11, 1995.
So far, Lombard’s first experience in the majors has been uneven.
Advertisement
Entering Monday, he was hitting just .215 with three home runs, 11 RBIs and a .619 OPS. His 73 wRC+ was sixth worst among shortstops with at least 100 plate appearances. Lombard homered in his first game in the majors, but has often swung and missed (25.9 percent) and he hasn’t exactly been crushing the baseball (85.5 mph average exit velocity).
Defensively, Lombard has looked more than capable, displaying a strong arm, good range and smooth actions. But he also had a stretch in which he made an error in six straight games. At the time, it was the longest consecutive error streak since Cleveland’s Mark Lewis had an error in seven straight games in 1992.
Lombard’s simply wanting a chance to ask Jeter questions that would prepare him for life as the Yankees’ shortstop was impressive, manager Aaron Boone said.
“I love when our players have an interest in connecting themselves to the organization,” Boone said. “Doing something like that and going and talking to Derek — those are cool things, when your players are curious. Look, everyone’s not that way. You respect that. But you do love when guys are curious and understand the magnitude of this organization and wanting to be an important part of it.”
Jeter returned to Yankee Stadium on Friday for the 25th anniversary of 9/11. While he was there, he visited the Yankees’ clubhouse and reconnected with Lombard. This time, it wasn’t over breakfast, but at a big-league ballpark.
“It’s been kind of a crazy year,” Lombard said. “But he’s happy for me, and he told me to keep doing my thing and to stay focused.”
Just another slice of advice to Lombard from Jeter, who knows what he’s talking about.
